title: With a Better Understanding of Physics, We Could Predict Volcanic Eruptions
gist: A Quanta Magazine feature (republished in Wired) surveys volcanologists arguing that eruption forecasting remains decades behind weather forecasting because scientists still lack the underlying physics of magma-reservoir failure, not just data; new efforts combining machine learning, dense seismic networks, geochemistry, and the world's first direct magma observatory (Iceland's Krafla Magma Testbed) aim to derive shared 'volcano archetype' equations that could eventually enable weeks-ahead eruption forecasts.

themes.theme: Why eruption forecasting lags weather forecasting

insights.claim: Unlike weather, which is perpetually occurring and continuously measurable, magma resides kilometers below the crust and most active volcanoes erupt only once every few decades, meaning volcanologists have vastly fewer opportunities to observe the phenomenon they are trying to forecast.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews (citing Jenni Barclay)
insights.so_what: The fundamental data-scarcity problem (rare eruption events vs. continuous weather) explains why eruption forecasting cannot simply replicate weather-forecasting methodology and instead requires new observational infrastructure built over decades.
insights.quote: The big difference between [volcanoes] and the weather forecasting is the weather is always happening... Magma, on the other hand, resides kilometers below Earth's crust, and at most, active volcanoes erupt once every few decades.

insights.claim: Every volcano is architecturally and chemically unique — differing in subterranean magma pathway structure, magma chemistry, eruption cadence, and eruption style — and eruptions have no single trigger, since magma temperature/pressure, surrounding rock weakness, gas and crystal content, magma depth, and regional tectonic motion all interact to determine whether an eruption occurs.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: Establishes the core scientific challenge as multi-causal and heterogeneous across sites, meaning any predictive model must account for numerous interacting variables rather than a single triggering signal — informs why a generalized 'archetype' modeling approach is being pursued.
insights.quote: The temperature and pressure of the magma reservoir, the weakness of the enclosing rock, the gas and crystal content, the depth of the magma, the regional motion of tectonic plates—these factors all contribute to whether a paroxysm happens or fizzles out.

insights.claim: The core unsolved scientific problem is that researchers still do not fully understand the underlying physics of what causes a magma reservoir to transition from a stable state to catastrophic failure; existing warning systems rely on correlating measurable geophysical signals (like escalating seismicity) with eruptions, but correlation is insufficient for prediction because these patterns are not always consistent.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews (citing Diana Roman and Jessica Johnson)
insights.so_what: Reframes the eruption-forecasting problem as fundamentally a physics-knowledge gap rather than a data or instrumentation gap — the key thesis of the entire article and the rationale for new multi-decade physics-focused research programs.
insights.quote: We don't even fully understand the underlying physics... What causes a magma reservoir to transition from a stable state to catastrophic failure?

insights.claim: Current volcanic unrest alert systems, including those used by the US Geological Survey, are unreliable predictors of actual eruption: only about 50 percent of volcanic unrest that appears likely to lead to an eruption actually results in one.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews (citing Jessica Johnson)
insights.so_what: A concrete 50% false-positive-adjacent rate on unrest-to-eruption alerts is a hard benchmark showing current volcanic warning systems function closer to a coin flip than a reliable forecast, quantifying just how far the field is from weather-forecast-level accuracy.
insights.quote: Only 50 percent of volcanic unrest that looks like it's going to be an eruption ends up in an eruption.

insights.claim: Some volcanic eruptions occur with no discernible warning signs at all: pressurized water pockets trapped near the surface, heated by adjacent magma, can rupture into a sudden steam explosion that then releases the underlying magma, functioning like a land mine next to a buried mountain of dynamite even at heavily instrumented volcanoes.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific eruption mechanism (phreatic/steam explosions from pressurized water pockets) that defeats even comprehensive monitoring, marking a category of risk that current forecasting approaches cannot address regardless of instrumentation density.
insights.quote: Pockets of highly pressurized water trapped just below the surface can be heated by adjacent bodies of magma. If that pocket ruptures, a dangerous steam explosion follows... This type of eruption often occurs with no discernible warning signs.

insights.claim: At frequently active, well-studied volcanoes like Italy's Stromboli and Etna, scientists can confidently forecast an eruption several hours in advance, and at Hawaii's Kīlauea and Iceland's Reykjanes Peninsula, seismology and ground-deformation tracking allow scientists to predict where migrating magma will surface as lava to within about an hour — but such precision is 'relatively unusual' and limited to frequently erupting, generally non-explosive volcanoes.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews (citing Maurizio Ripepe and Tom Winder)
insights.so_what: Establishes the current best-case forecasting capability (hours-to-an-hour precision) as achievable only for a narrow class of frequently active, well-monitored, effusive volcanoes — a baseline against which future forecasting advances should be measured.
insights.quote: We have systems that can tell us that in a few hours, the volcano will erupt... scientists at other volcanoes, including Hawaii's Kīlauea and those on Iceland's Reykjanes Peninsula, can track magma migrating underground with such staggering precision that they know exactly where it will emerge as lava, to within an hour or so.
insights.locator: Paragraphs on Stromboli, Etna, Kīlauea, Reykjanes

insights.claim: Scientists have already derived successful physics-based models — including application of the Navier-Stokes equations (fluid movement) and the heat equation (cooling rates) — that predict where lava and pyroclastic flows will travel, how far, and how fast, once an eruption has already begun, but this only addresses the aftermath of eruption onset, not the harder problem of predicting when an eruption will start.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews (citing Mike Poland)
insights.so_what: Draws a clear boundary between solved (post-eruption flow physics) and unsolved (pre-eruption trigger physics) problems in volcanology, clarifying exactly where future research investment needs to be directed.
insights.quote: Using our weather analogy, this is like saying, 'Once the rain starts to fall, we can forecast what watersheds might flood.' Knowing when the storm will start requires getting at the subsurface physics of magma reservoirs.
insights.locator: Mike Poland quote on Navier-Stokes application

themes.theme: New research infrastructure aimed at cracking the physics

insights.claim: A new multidisciplinary project called Ex-X ('Expecting the Unexpected'), led by the University of Bristol, is deploying hundreds of seismometers and fiber-optic cable networks across Eastern Caribbean volcanoes to record even the tiniest earthquakes during calm and unrest periods, aided by machine learning trained to detect minute shifts in seismic signals, with the goal of uncovering shared fluid-dynamics physics across these diverse volcanoes.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews (citing Jessica Johnson)
insights.so_what: A concrete, named, currently-running research program (Ex-X) using dense seismic/fiber-optic networks plus ML is a specific initiative to track for near-term breakthroughs in volcanic physics understanding.
insights.quote: As part of this work, hundreds of seismometers, as well as networks of fiber-optic cables, will be used to record even the tiniest of earthquakes during periods of tranquility and unrest.

insights.claim: Machine learning programs are already processing volcanic seismic data far more proficiently than scientists working alone, having already revealed previously hidden magmatic pathways beneath volcanoes and enabling near-real-time tracking of magma movement through the crust.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: Machine learning is already delivering measurable gains in volcanic monitoring (discovering hidden pathways, near-real-time tracking), positioning ML-driven seismic analysis as a proven near-term lever for improving eruption forecasting ahead of a full physics breakthrough.
insights.quote: In recent years, these programs have been used to process a huge volume of data far more proficiently and efficiently than scientists can manage alone. This work has already revealed myriad previously hidden magmatic pathways beneath volcanoes.
insights.locator: Paragraph on machine learning role in Ex-X

insights.claim: Iceland's Krafla Magma Testbed is set to become the world's first direct magma observatory, aiming to drill down to where magma sits at depth so scientists can observe magmatic processes in situ rather than only inferring them from surface results.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews (citing Tom Winder)
insights.so_what: A first-of-its-kind direct magma observatory is a landmark infrastructure investment that could be the single biggest unlock for validating physics-based eruption models, worth tracking for its findings' downstream effect on volcano hazard science.
insights.quote: Drill all the way down to where there is some magma sitting at depth, and really see these processes in situ, rather than just seeing the results of them... That is one of the objectives of the Krafla Magma Testbed in Iceland. This literally groundbreaking facility is set to become the world's first direct magma observatory.

insights.claim: In successful laboratory experiments in fall 2025, scientists recreated the extreme conditions present at the birth of planets, including simulated magma and miniature hydrogen atmospheres, representing meaningful progress toward laboratory replication of magma-chamber-like conditions that were previously impossible to simulate.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews (citing Mike Poland)
insights.so_what: A specific, dated 2025 laboratory milestone (recreating planet-formation conditions) shows tangible progress in experimental capability that could soon allow direct laboratory validation of magma-chamber behavior models.
insights.quote: In successful experiments in the fall of 2025, scientists re-created the conditions present at the birth of planets, complete with simulacra of magma and miniature hydrogen atmospheres.

insights.claim: The proposed international Subduction Zones in Four Dimensions (SZ4D) project, if sufficiently funded, would conduct an intense, multi-decade monitoring campaign across subduction zones including Chile, Alaska, and the Cascades to study the shared physics driving major landslides, earthquakes, and eruptions.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews (citing Diana Roman)
insights.so_what: A proposed, funding-contingent, multi-decade international monitoring project (SZ4D) is the type of 'geologic Manhattan Project' scale investment the article's sources say is necessary — its funding status is a leading indicator of whether the field commits to solving the physics gap.
insights.quote: SZ4D would be a colossal scientific undertaking. But similarly mammoth endeavors were needed to understand how the weather works, and how Earth's climate is rapidly changing. You've got to start somewhere. 'It's time for a big push,' Roman says.

themes.theme: The long-term vision: an archetypal volcano model

insights.claim: The long-term vision is to derive shared, foundational geophysical equations across many volcanoes and build a generic 'archetypal volcano model' that could be applied to any specific volcano — for example, feeding Japan's Mount Fuji's current seismicity, magmatic geochemistry, and deformation rate into the model to virtually forecast its most probable eruption date, style, and duration; some experts suspect there may be multiple distinct volcano archetypes (e.g., lava-dominant vs. explosive).
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews (citing Zach Ross)
insights.so_what: Defines the field's endgame model architecture (a generalizable archetype model transferable across specific volcanoes) that, if achieved, would be the volcanology equivalent of general-purpose weather models — a long-horizon scientific milestone with major public-safety implications.
insights.quote: Software driven by those governing equations could then virtually fast-forward the volcano toward its most probable eruption date, while also describing the likeliest eruption style and duration... That's definitely the right way to be thinking about it.
insights.locator: Zach Ross quote near end of article

insights.claim: Roughly 800 million people live within 100 kilometers of an active volcano, and even many of the most dangerous US volcanoes along the Cascades (including Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier) remain only partly covered by monitoring sensors, with true continuous, permanent monitoring networks existing at only a 'handful of Cadillac volcanoes' worldwide.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews (citing Diana Roman)
insights.so_what: An at-risk population of 800 million juxtaposed against sparse global monitoring infrastructure (even for dangerous US volcanoes like Rainier) underscores a major public-safety and infrastructure-investment gap independent of the unsolved physics problem.
insights.quote: Even many of the United States' most dangerous volcanoes, along the Cascades in the Pacific Northwest (home to the notorious Mount St. Helens, for example, and the precarious Mount Rainier), are only partly covered in a limited number of sensors.

insights.claim: Views on the feasibility of weather-like eruption forecasting split among experts: some, like Diana Roman, are confidently optimistic that shared underlying physics can eventually be found across all volcanoes, while others, like Tom Winder, remain skeptical it will work beyond exceptional cases like Hawaii or Iceland's most frequently active volcanoes.
insights.speaker: Robin George Andrews
insights.so_what: Documents genuine expert disagreement on forecasting feasibility, useful for calibrating expectations: the field is not unanimous that weather-style eruption forecasting is achievable even with better funding and instrumentation.
insights.quote: At the moment, I can only imagine it in exceptional circumstances... citing volcanoes that erupt with great frequency, like those in Hawaii or Iceland.
